supplement.holds: Appendix A: participant demographics (Table 3, p. 26); B: task-duration distributions (Figure 6, p. 27); C: lexical frequency profiles with SEM bands (Figure 7, p. 28); D: assistant system prompts (pp. 26-29); E: a sample conversation transcript (pp. 29-31). paper_design_summary: Prolific participants wrote an argumentative essay with no AI, immediate generative chatbot access, engagement-gated access, or time-matched access; only the first three conditions were randomly assigned, while the time-matched condition was recruited in a separate phase (pp. 5-7). The final essays were scored for semantic dispersion, semantic location, lexical reuse, length, and argumentative structure, with a separately generated AI-only reference corpus (pp. 8-9, 12-15). The same participants then evaluated source-based passages without AI; this assessed error detection and classification rather than creative production (pp. 7 and 10).

studies.label: Argumentative writing experiment: randomized first phase and separately recruited time-matched second phase

assignment.what_was_assigned: Phase 1 participants were randomly assigned to Human-Only, Standard Chatbot, or Engage-to-Unlock. A separately recruited Phase 2 sample, excluding Phase 1 participants, was assigned entirely to Time-Matched Unlock and yoked to recorded Engage-to-Unlock schedules. Thus online_rct applies to comparisons among the three Phase 1 arms only; any contrast involving Time-Matched Unlock is quasi_people (observational context), not randomized. The AI-only reference was not assigned to people or an experimental arm.

arms.name: Standard Chatbot

arms.name: Engage-to-Unlock

participants.exclusions: Of 445 session completers, 398 were analyzed after passing both embedded attention checks; numbers originally assigned and pre-exclusion arm counts are not reported (p. 6). Six internal pilot sessions were excluded from the main analysis (p. 7). Analyses retained the attention-check-passing participants with unlock-delivery deviations (p. 8); the timer problem affected 14 Time-Matched Unlock participants (p. 11). The analysis follows attention-check exclusions; the paper does not establish that every randomized participant was retained.

ai_tool.how_used: A conversational writing assistant could see the live essay, conversation history, and reference sources. The single role code other represents the combination of coach and open_chat policies: Teach-me supplied process guidance and was instructed not to contribute task-specific argumentative content or draft prose; Tell-me could supply ideas, reasoning, organization, revisions, and draftable prose. Both modes used the same gemini-3.1-pro-preview model and conversation context. Standard Chatbot used Tell-me throughout; Engage-to-Unlock and Time-Matched Unlock began with Teach-me and could later switch to Tell-me. AI remained available during writing even without generation unlock: 98 of 107 analyzed Engage-to-Unlock participants and 60 of 94 analyzed Time-Matched Unlock participants received Tell-me access before submission. Task 2 had no AI assistance (pp. 5-7, sections 3.1-3.4; p. 11, section 4.1.1; pp. 26-29, Appendix D).

task.description: Task 1: write at least 200 words about the four-day workweek using four source summaries, two supportive and two critical, with source order counterbalanced. The essay task qualifies through its across-writer diversity measure; no human-rated overall creativity or novelty outcome is reported. Task 2 subsequently required evaluating eight 150-word AI-generated passages without AI; it was an error-evaluation task, not a further creative-writing task (p. 7).
task.duration: Each task had a suggested duration of 20 minutes, but participants worked at their own pace; study approximately one hour (pp. 6-7).

diversity_detail.metric: D_c = mean squared Euclidean distance to the condition centroid; HI_c = 1 - D_c / D_Human-Only.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Gemini Embedding 2; 3,072-dimensional vectors; SEMANTIC_SIMILARITY task type (p. 9, section 3.5.3).
diversity_detail.computed_over: One complete final essay per writer, compared with the centroid of the essays in that same condition after whitespace normalization. This is dispersion across different writers, not variation within one writer (p. 9, section 3.5.3).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Within-condition 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals from 5,000 resamples. The resampling unit is not explicitly identified beyond the essay-based dispersion calculation. No bootstrap interval for the arm difference, participant-level contrast SE, or formal difference/equivalence test is supplied (pp. 9 and 13).
diversity_detail.notes: Larger D_c means greater diversity. Larger HI_c means greater homogenization, so its interpretation is reversed for an atlas effect favoring diversity; no effect or sign-transformed number was computed. The no_clear_difference codes reflect the descriptive analysis and absence of a formal contrast, not evidence of equivalence. The text explicitly distinguishes PCA location from diversity (p. 9). Table 1's printed homogenization indices are retained without recomputing them from rounded dispersion estimates.

outcomes.name: Semantic location of essays (joint PCA component scores)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Exploratory joint PCA of L2-normalized embeddings from participant and AI-only essays (498 essays; p. 9, section 3.5.3). Components are retained together as the semantic-location analysis. The paper explicitly says PCA measures location rather than diversity. PC1 explains 17.91% of variance; PC2 4.44%; PC3 3.61%. PCA coordinate direction has no inherent better-creativity interpretation. t-SNE is visualization only, not another diversity endpoint. Measure coding: null because the current measure vocabulary has no code for PCA component scores. embedding_similarity denotes distances between embeddings, whereas this outcome compares component scores and condition means to describe semantic location (creativity-codebook.md, section 6).

eligibility.reason: Phase 1 randomly assigned individual writers to Human-Only, Standard Chatbot, or Engage-to-Unlock (p. 6, sections 3.1-3.2; p. 20, section 5.3). These arms analyzed 99, 98, and 107 people, respectively, and thus exceed the 50-person criterion without the 94 analyzed nonrandom Phase 2 participants; 398 is the total analyzed across both phases, not a randomized count (p. 6, section 3.2; p. 26, Table 3). Semantic dispersion is computed across different writers' complete final essays and reported by condition with bootstrap intervals, satisfying the output-scored diversity criterion (p. 9, section 3.5.3, equations (1)-(2); p. 13, Table 1). Only comparisons among the Phase 1 arms qualify as randomized evidence. Time-Matched Unlock comparisons remain nonrandom context, and the AI-only corpus is a descriptive reference. Correcting the ancillary word-count, PCA-location, and word-frequency measure labels does not change eligibility. The later passage-evaluation task is not a creative-production outcome. Missing assignment-stage counts and contrast precision do not prevent any eligibility criterion from being met.

one_line_finding: Among 398 analyzed writers, essay semantic dispersion was descriptively similar across conditions (Human-Only 0.179, Engage-to-Unlock 0.187, Standard Chatbot 0.188, Time-Matched Unlock 0.188), without a formal between-condition test (p. 6, section 3.2; p. 13, Table 1; p. 9, section 3.5.3).
open_questions: Assignment-stage totals, phase-specific pre-exclusion counts, and per-arm attention-check exclusions are not reported; 445 is the session-completer count, not a randomized count (p. 6, section 3.2).

The methods promise discourse differences, SEs, degrees of freedom, and CIs (p. 8), but most discourse outcomes lack these numerical results in the main text and included appendices. No external supplement or data/code repository is identified.

Dispersion has condition-level bootstrap intervals, but no arm-difference SE or interval and no formal between-condition test; the precise bootstrap resampling procedure is not specified (p. 9, section 3.5.3; p. 13, Table 1).
notes: Both raw forms parsed. The complete markdown, including references and appendices A-E, was read in contiguous chunks. All retained numerical results were checked against PDF text; Tables 1 and 2 were also inspected with PyMuPDF table extraction. One study represents the paper's two-phase experiment. The online_rct designation and core eligibility apply only to comparisons among Human-Only, Standard Chatbot, and Engage-to-Unlock in Phase 1. Every comparison involving the separately recruited Time-Matched Unlock cohort is nonrandom and must remain observational context. The AI-only reference and internal pilots are not additional randomized participant arms. The AI-only reference comprises 100 independently generated essays (p. 8); Table 1 gives D_c = 0.065 [0.061, 0.068] and HI_c = +0.636 (+63.6%) relative to Human-Only (p. 13). Table 2 reports AI-only length 495.5 +/- 38.3 words, source coverage 2.03% +/- 1.59%, and source-match prevalence 74.0% (p. 15). These are descriptive reference-corpus statistics, not assistance effects. All twelve source-supported output measures are retained, including the six ancillary outcomes listed only by B. Only semantic dispersion establishes the creativity/diversity output criterion. Other measures describe length, argumentative structure, semantic location, vocabulary, or text incorporation and are not validated creativity or novelty scores. Under the form's question rule, assisted non-diversity output measures are labeled with_ai; that label alone does not establish a creativity benefit or eligibility for pooling. Discourse elements and rhetorical category counts are coded other. PCA components are grouped as one location analysis, and HI_c is grouped with dispersion. The PCA analysis includes the AI-only corpus; its 498 essays are outputs, not people (p. 9). open_items.item: Assignment-stage totals, phase-specific pre-exclusion counts, and per-arm attention-check exclusions are not reported; 445 is the session-completer count, not a randomized count (p. 6, section 3.2). Authors would need to supply assignment and exclusion counts by phase and arm, including any losses before completion. This does not affect criteria 1 or 2: random assignment in Phase 1 and sufficient analyzed people are explicit; it does not concern criterion 3.

The methods promise discourse differences, SEs, degrees of freedom, and CIs (p. 8), but most discourse outcomes lack these numerical results in the main text and included appendices. No external supplement or data/code repository is identified. Authors would need to supply the missing discourse arm summaries and contrast estimates with precision. No eligibility criterion depends on these ancillary discourse statistics; criterion 3 is established by final-essay semantic dispersion.

Dispersion has condition-level bootstrap intervals, but no arm-difference SE or interval and no formal between-condition test; the precise bootstrap resampling procedure is not specified (p. 9, section 3.5.3; p. 13, Table 1). Authors would need to identify the bootstrap resampling unit and procedure and provide arm-difference uncertainty or the data and code needed to estimate it. This affects extraction and pooling, not criteria 1-3; an output-scored diversity measure is present even without a formal between-condition test.
